analyses.title: Cross-document event ordering through temporal, lexical and distributional knowledge
analyses.research_question: Can temporal compatibility, lexical-semantic knowledge, and distributional-semantic knowledge be combined to improve cross-document event coreference and chronological timeline construction from multiple texts?
analyses.methodology: The system constructs entity-centered event timelines from multiple English news documents by combining event extraction, temporal information processing, target-entity filtering, and cross-document event coreference. It clusters event mentions using temporal compatibility and then semantic compatibility derived from lexical-semantic and distributional-semantic knowledge, treating word meaning and contextual usage as complementary signals. System variants are evaluated using the SemEval-2015 Task 4 TimeLine framework, with an additional experiment using manual MEANTIME entity-coreference annotations to analyze error propagation from entity resolution.

key_findings.finding: Combining temporal, lexical-semantic, and distributional-semantic knowledge improved the cross-document event-ordering results over previously evaluated systems, with gains reported as high as eight F1 points.
The best configuration continued to be the combination of temporal, lexical, and distributional semantics when manual entity-coreference annotations were substituted for automatic entity coreference.

With manual MEANTIME entity coreference, the combined configuration reached micro-F1 30.09, precision 25.37, and recall 36.98; relative to the best automatic-entity-coreference setup, the paper reports gains of 3.5 F1 points, 1.7 precision points, and 6.61 recall points.
Entity-coreference quality is an important upstream bottleneck because correcting it manually particularly increases event recall in the resulting timelines.
Nominal event mentions such as deverbal nouns remain difficult to match with verbal mentions, creating cross-document event-coreference errors.

limitations: The experiments focus on written English news, so transfer to workplace email, chat, and conversational communication is not evaluated.
The model orders and corefers events but does not explicitly represent factuality states such as planned, uncertain, confirmed, revoked, completed, or contradicted.
The pipeline is vulnerable to upstream errors in event extraction, temporal anchoring, named-entity recognition, and entity coreference.
Nominal events and lexical variation can prevent mentions of the same real-world event from being clustered together.
The approach does not model chronological revisions of an event's asserted status, such as a plan later being canceled or corrected.
raw_claims: Cross-document event ordering requires event extraction, temporal relation processing, and cross-document event coreference.
The system uses temporal, lexical-semantic, and distributional-semantic information when constructing timelines.
Temporal compatibility is treated as necessary evidence when deciding whether event mentions may corefer.
Lexical semantics and distributional semantics supply complementary notions of semantic compatibility.
The approach was evaluated in the SemEval-2015 TimeLine cross-document event-ordering framework.
The reported system improves the previously evaluated systems by as much as eight F1 points.
Using manually annotated entity coreference substantially improves recall.
The combined temporal, lexical, and distributional configuration remains the best configuration with manual entity coreference.
The manual-coreference version of the combined model obtains micro-F1 30.09.
Deverbal nominal events are identified as a source of coreference errors.

analyses.title: FactBank: a corpus annotated with event factuality
analyses.research_question: How can event factuality be represented and reliably annotated as source-relative combinations of polarity and epistemic certainty in text?
analyses.methodology: The authors define event factuality as the commitment of relevant discourse sources toward the factual status of events and construct a discrete annotation framework combining polarity with degrees of epistemic certainty. FactBank adds this semantic layer to TimeBank and a subset of the AQUAINT TimeML corpus, yielding 208 documents and 9,488 manually annotated events. Annotation is decomposed into identifying source-introducing predicates, identifying relevant sources, and assigning factuality values, with copredication-based diagnostic tests used to distinguish modality levels. Inter-annotator agreement is measured separately for the three annotation tasks.

key_findings.finding: FactBank contains 208 documents and 9,488 manually annotated events drawn from TimeBank and a subset of the AQUAINT TimeML corpus.

The factuality representation combines positive, negative, or underspecified polarity with certain, probable, possible, or underspecified modality, thereby distinguishing facts, counterfacts, uncertainty, and non-commitment.

Inter-annotator agreement was high for the annotation decomposition: Cohen's kappa was 0.88 for source-introducing predicates, 0.95 for source identification, and 0.81 for factuality-value assignment.
The corpus explicitly represents factuality relative to relevant sources rather than treating factuality as a single source-independent truth value.
The annotation deliberately excludes factuality changes that require multiple sentences, even though the authors note that an initially uncommitted event may later be presented as a fact.
The AQUAINT portion is strongly skewed: 58.1% of annotated values are certain-positive and 36.6% are fully underspecified, while lower-certainty or non-positive categories are comparatively rare.

limitations: Factuality judgments are intentionally constrained to sentence-level information, so cross-sentence revisions and state changes are not annotated.
FactBank contains English news-style material rather than workplace email or dialogue.
The annotation represents textual source commitment, not independent verification that an event actually occurred.
Rare probable, possible, and negative factuality categories produce a highly imbalanced label distribution.
The framework does not directly encode operational lifecycle states such as planned, scheduled, completed, revoked, superseded, or reopened.
A discourse model for tracking changing factuality across sentences is identified as necessary but is outside the corpus annotation design.
raw_claims: Event factuality is defined in terms of a source's commitment toward the factual nature of an event.
Factuality varies along polarity and certainty dimensions.
The scheme distinguishes certain, probable, possible, and underspecified modality.
FactBank contains 208 documents and 9,488 manually annotated events.
FactBank is layered on top of existing TimeML-annotated material.
Annotation first identifies source-introducing predicates and relevant sources before assigning factuality.
Cohen's kappa for factuality-value assignment is 0.81.
An event can be introduced without commitment and later be characterized as factual in subsequent discourse.
The released annotation nevertheless restricts factuality judgments to the containing sentence.
Certain-positive and fully underspecified values dominate the AQUAINT portion of the corpus.
The authors state that FactBank is to be made available through the Linguistic Data Consortium.

analyses.title: End-to-end event factuality prediction using directional labeled graph recurrent network
analyses.research_question: Can event anchors and their factuality scores be predicted jointly from plain sentences while improving factuality estimation through directional and labeled syntactic graph information?
analyses.methodology: The paper formulates end-to-end event factuality prediction as joint Event Anchor Detection and Factuality Induction rather than assuming gold event-anchor positions. DLGRN constructs a graph over sentence words using directional labeled dependency edges together with sequential edges and self-loops, initializes contextual representations with BERT, and performs recurrent graph message passing using edge-tied weights and edge-aware attention. Shared representations feed separate anchor-detection and factuality-regression heads in a multi-task objective, with factuality represented on a continuous scale from -3 to +3. The model is evaluated on the publicly accessible FactBank, Meantime, UW, and UDS-IH2 benchmarks using anchor-detection metrics plus MAE and Pearson correlation for factuality.

key_findings.finding: Across the four benchmarks, DLGRN is reported to reduce MAE by an average of 17.12% and increase Pearson correlation by 5.40% relative to the strongest baseline.

DLGRN achieved the best factuality-induction values in the reported comparison on all four datasets, including MAE/correlation pairs of 0.240/0.912 on FactBank, 0.279/0.516 on Meantime, 0.346/0.863 on UW, and 0.722/0.912 on UDS-IH2.

The UW ablation shows labeled syntactic information as the most consequential tested graph component: removing it changes F1 from 0.91 to 0.89, MCC from 0.883 to 0.745, MAE from 0.346 to 0.422, and correlation from 0.863 to 0.788.
Removing multi-task learning and reverting toward a pipeline setup degrades both event-anchor detection and factuality induction, supporting shared learning between the two subtasks.
DLGRN outperforms the compared GCN and GAT-LSTM systems across sentence-length buckets, with larger correlation gaps in the longest buckets.
The narrative claim that DLGRN has fewer parameters than all baselines is contradicted by the paper's own tables, which list BERT at 109.5M parameters and DLGRN at 119.7M.

limitations: The model operates on individual sentences and therefore does not track factuality revisions across messages, sentences, or document versions.
Dependency parses are part of graph construction, so syntactic parsing errors can propagate into factuality predictions.
Only factuality scores for correctly identified event anchors are included in the factuality-induction evaluation, making that evaluation conditional on successful anchor detection.
Predicted factuality ranges are narrower than the gold ranges, and the paper reports difficulty producing scores near the extremes.
The authors note biased factuality distributions in the smaller FactBank and Meantime datasets.
A scalar factuality score does not explicitly distinguish workflow states such as planned, confirmed, canceled, completed, or superseded.
The evaluation benchmarks do not establish performance on workplace communication.
raw_claims: End-to-end EFP takes plain text rather than gold event-anchor positions as input.
DLGRN jointly performs Event Anchor Detection and Factuality Induction.
The graph preserves dependency direction and dependency labels.
Sequential edges and self-loops are added to the syntactic graph.
BERT contextual embeddings initialize the word representations.
Factuality induction is formulated as regression over scores from -3 to +3.
Experiments use FactBank, Meantime, UW, and UDS-IH2.
DLGRN reports lower MAE and higher Pearson correlation than the compared methods on all four datasets.
Removing labeled edge information produces the largest degradation among the reported graph-information ablations on UW.
The model's predicted score ranges are narrower than the gold-score ranges.
DLGRN performs comparatively well on longer sentences.
The paper's parameter-count table contradicts its prose claim that DLGRN is smaller than every baseline.

analyses.title: Document-Level Event Factuality Identification via Reinforced Semantic Learning Network
analyses.research_question: Can document-level event factuality be identified end to end by jointly encoding event and document semantics while learning to select the sentences and tokens most relevant to the target event?
analyses.methodology: The paper formulates document-level event factuality identification as assigning a document-wide factuality value to a target event even when sentences mentioning or discussing it carry differing local factuality. RSLN uses multi-granularity hierarchical semantic encoding together with hierarchical reinforcement learning to select event-relevant sentences and tokens while filtering irrelevant or noisy text. Its encoders combine event information, intra-sentence semantics, and document-topic information before producing the document-level prediction. The model is evaluated on the newly annotated English and Chinese ExDLEF corpus and compared with multiple neural baselines, with additional component ablations and text-selection analyses.

key_findings.finding: The paper explicitly observes that sentence-level factualities concerning an event may differ within a document while defining the document-level factuality as a single value.
On ExDLEF, RSLN reports macro/micro F1 of 67.42/77.48 for English and 75.74/78.29 for Chinese, outperforming the reported comparison systems.
Ablation results identify the event encoder and topic-context encoder as two of the most important components: removing them produces substantial macro- and micro-F1 losses in both languages.

Sentence selection has a larger measured effect than token selection: removing SPNet reduces macro-F1 by 4.07 points in English and 4.64 in Chinese, compared with 1.35 and 0.85 points when TPNet is removed.
ExDLEF contains 5,030 English instances and 5,150 Chinese instances across Uu, CT-, PS-, PS+, and CT+ factuality categories.
The paper identifies insufficient direct evaluation of selected-sentence quality and limited deep interpretability of the model as an experimental limitation.

limitations: The model assigns one document-level factuality value, so differing local mentions are collapsed rather than preserved as an explicit temporal revision trajectory.
The authors identify inadequate direct evaluation of selected sentences and limited deep interpretability as limitations.
Multi-event document-level factuality and cross-document factuality are left for future work.
ExDLEF is highly imbalanced; for example, the English portion contains 3,532 CT+ instances but only 42 Uu and 51 PS- instances.
The main reported per-class F1 comparisons emphasize CT-, PS+, and CT+, giving much less empirical evidence about the rare factuality categories.
The formulation does not explicitly encode workflow transitions such as planned-to-confirmed, planned-to-canceled, completed-to-corrected, or superseded-by-later-message.
Performance on workplace email and dialogue is not evaluated.
raw_claims: Document-level event factuality is defined from the perspective of the whole document.
Sentence-level factuality values for the same target event may differ within a document.
RSLN selects relevant sentences and tokens using hierarchical reinforcement learning.
The representation combines event, sentence-level, and document-level semantic information.
ExDLEF contains both English and Chinese sub-corpora.
The English ExDLEF portion contains 5,030 instances and the Chinese portion contains 5,150.
RSLN reaches macro-F1 67.42 and micro-F1 77.48 on the English ExDLEF evaluation.
RSLN reaches macro-F1 75.74 and micro-F1 78.29 on the Chinese ExDLEF evaluation.
Event and topic-context encoders make large contributions in the ablation study.
Sentence selection has a larger ablation effect than token selection.
The paper does not precisely evaluate the performance of its selected sentences or provide deep model interpretability.
The authors identify multi-event, evidential, and cross-document event factuality as future research directions.

analyses.title: Utilizing Relative Event Time to Enhance Event-Event Temporal Relation Extraction
analyses.research_question: Can latent relative event times learned from temporal-relation supervision improve event-event temporal relation extraction when explicit event-time expressions are sparse?
analyses.methodology: The model starts with RoBERTa-based contextual representations for a pair of supplied event mentions and jointly learns temporal-relation classification and an auxiliary relative-event-time prediction task. Each event receives a learned real-valued relative timestamp, and relation-specific objectives encourage BEFORE events to be ordered in one direction, AFTER events in the reverse direction, and EQUAL events to receive similar times. Stack-Propagation feeds the predicted relative times back into the relation classifier while retaining differentiability so relation-classification gradients also update the timing component. Evaluation uses MATRES with TimeBank and AQUAINT for training, a 21-document development split, Platinum for testing, five random seeds, and F1 as the primary relation-extraction metric.

key_findings.finding: The Stack-Propagation model reaches precision 78.4, recall 85.2, and F1 81.7 on MATRES, compared with F1 80.2 for the vanilla RoBERTa classifier; the paper reports p<0.05 for the comparison.
The proposed model slightly exceeds the reported 81.6 F1 of the self-training baseline while not using that baseline's additional annotated and raw training resources.
Relative-time prediction alone in the multi-task configuration improves F1 from 80.2 to 80.6, while explicitly propagating predicted times into classification raises F1 further to 81.7.
Deriving relations by directly comparing predicted timestamps yields the highest recall, 86.8, but only F1 80.7 because this strategy cannot adequately handle VAGUE relations.
Predicted relative-time differences correlate with BEFORE and AFTER decisions, while VAGUE and EQUAL pairs tend to have relative-time differences near zero.
The paper releases a public implementation and resources repository for the method.

limitations: The experiments use MATRES, whose documents are news-derived, and do not test workplace email or dialogue.
The model extracts temporal relations rather than factuality or operational states, so it cannot by itself distinguish planned, confirmed, revoked, completed, or contradicted events.
Event mentions are supplied to the relation model rather than detected as part of a fully end-to-end event-tracking pipeline.
The relative timestamps are latent bounded values rather than calibrated calendar times.
VAGUE is treated as no relation in evaluation and receives no direct relative-time ordering constraint comparable to BEFORE, AFTER, or EQUAL.
Cross-document temporal reasoning is explicitly left for future work.
Pairwise temporal ordering does not itself resolve conflicting factual revisions about whether an event will or did occur.
raw_claims: Explicit event-time links are sparse in temporal corpora.
The paper learns a real-valued relative time for each event.
Relative-event-time prediction is trained jointly with event-event temporal relation classification.
Stack-Propagation supplies predicted event times directly to the temporal-relation classifier.
MATRES is used for the main evaluation.
The reported MATRES split contains 260 training documents, 21 development documents, and 20 test documents.
The proposed model obtains 81.7 F1 averaged over five random seeds.
The vanilla classifier obtains 80.2 F1 in the ablation comparison.
Direct timestamp comparison has high recall but has difficulty representing VAGUE relations.
BEFORE and AFTER predictions correlate with the sign and magnitude of predicted relative-time differences.
VAGUE and EQUAL predictions tend to lie near zero relative-time difference.
The authors propose cross-document relative-time prediction and temporal-relation extraction as future work.
A public GitHub repository contains code and data resources for the paper.
